items.title: Anthropic Thunder
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
Following their big IPO, Anthropic’s 5,300 founders and employees were worth more than the bottom third of U.S. households. So what do these Ants (that’s what Anthropic employees call themselves) think of their new riches and their constantly renewing technology? Jasmine Sun spent a year talking to them to find out. Like the rest of us, they have worries. But they may not be the same worries. As with so many areas of today’s AI-driven tech world, there is a widening disconnect between the people who make the technology and the people they want to buy what they’re selling: “I have found them surprisingly earnest in their dedication to making AI go well. But their concerns are also idiosyncratic and insular, often far removed from the concerns that most people hold.” I Spent a Year Talking to Anthropic Employees. Here’s What They Believe. “Anthropic is about to become one of the most important companies of the 21st century. If it wants to steward our country, our economy and our lives, Anthropic must do much more to earn the public’s trust. We need a plan for how it will build AI safely, and not just a reliance on a few people’s judgment calls.”

+ A day after their much-anticipated, massive IPO, the Ants have something else to worry about. The stock is dropping like an An(t)vil. At the time of this writing, it’s hovering back around its IPO price, and the rest of the tech market is going down with it. “The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was off more than 3% and officially erasing all its previous gains in 2026.” This seems to break our unwritten agreement with AI companies. You can destroy humanity you can destroy our portfolios … but not both. If this market trend continues, even the Ants may be crying .

+ Of course, we can’t know all that much about what a company will become or be worth a few hours after its IPO. Robin Sloan puts things into perspective: “It’s instructive to think about Apple’s IPO in 1980, Amazon’s in 1997, Google’s in 2004 … all of them victory laps in their own way — yet those companies were, in those moments, barely premonitions of what they would become. Apple without the Mac or the iPhone; Amazon without AWS; Google without Chrome, YouTube, or, of course, Gemini. Thinking about Anthropic, it’s strange to imagine a product as profound and pathbreaking as Claude to be ‘merely’ its Apple II. Yet that’s surely correct.” (That said, there does seem to be a key difference in how we’re feeling right now. In the early days of Apple, Amazon, and Google, there was a sense of excitement about what we were making, while with AI, that excitement is mixed with a heavy helping of anxiety and even doom. Which reminds me, I better call my broker.)

“Trump’s chumminess with these men marks a low point in the history of the American presidency. He is insulting those who serve to protect the United States—too many of whom have been killed or seriously wounded because of China and Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the U.S.” Phillips Payson O’Brien in (Gift Article): Trump’s Axis of Ignorance.

+ “The President was alternately bedazzled by Xi’s tacky displays of hospitality and beaming at Putin like an octogenarian schoolboy with a crush, all while eagerly trading away America’s remaining credibility for a seat—and not even the best seat—at a table that no other American leader would have wanted to sit at.” Susan B. Glasser in : Two Autocrats and an American President with Autocrat Envy.

+ This is as bad as it sounds, and worse. I wrote about this yesterday. Trifect Up Beyond Repair. “My first thought upon watching the Trump/Xi/Putin dictators-in-triplicate fest was that it’s too bad the air travel ground stop didn’t last another week.”

From the : Threats, Insults, Settlements: How Jensen Huang Made Humiliation Routine. “He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.” (I can’t really point fingers on this one. NextDraft is fueled almost entirely by ritualistic humiliation, and I’m the only one who works here.)

+ We’re going to read a lot of stories about Jensen Huang and honey potting and Nvidia insider scoops. But don’t let that distract you from the bigger story; the one that explains why Huang still has a lot of support from some people in the administration. This story is not about a rogue CEO showing up in a hotel room to meet his girlfriend and hand over a briefcase filled with chips. It was a group effort. “Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced A.I. chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon … The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for the Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese A.I. firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said.” Trump hasn’t seen the need to call out or fire Howard Lutnick, the head of the Commerce Department. But he seemed fine with him coming along to hobnob with his business partners at this week’s APEC Summit in Shenzhen.

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell are both excellent in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine. If you’re looking for an excuse to hit the theater this holiday week, this is a great one.

+ “When rebellious Elisabeth falls for Emperor Franz and becomes his unlikely bride, she enters a world of tension and intrigue at the Viennese court.” The Empress is one of those international shows that has gone viral on Netflix. It’s like Gilded Age, but better.

Membership Has Its Rewards: “In 2023, Miller’s accountant put his total income at about $879,000. Then, Trump was elected president a second time. And Miller proceeded to make more money than he had in the previous seven years combined.” A child support fight exposed a Trump adviser’s $15 million income. (There will be examples like this bubbling up for years and years.)

+ “The US has carried out its first ever deep-sea mining lease sales off the coast of American Samoa, despite an adverse court ruling earlier this week and mounting local opposition.” The Pacific is not for sale. (The only way this month could be any worse for the administration would be if they pissed off Samoans.)

+ Every Rose Has Its Thorn: Pete Rose posthumously pardoned by President Donald Trump. Rose was a habitual liar who cheated on taxes, was accused of having sex with minors, and refused to apologize for his misdeeds. His nickname literally contained the word “hustle.” The only question is why Trump didn’t pardon him a long time ago.

+ You Can’t Play On Without Rayon: “The material in question wasn’t the breezy fabric in your favorite Hawaiian shirt. The Pentagon was focused instead on a carbonized version capable of withstanding temperatures in the thousands of degrees, which is critical for making high-end Patriot interceptors sought after around the world for missile defense.” The Pentagon Urgently Needs More Patriot Missiles. It’s Running Into a Rayon Problem.

+ “The U.S. Army’s plan to detonate five tons of unstable explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa has been put on indefinite hold by a federal court.”

items.title: Trifect Up Beyond Repair
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
My first thought upon watching the Trump/Xi/Putin dictators-in-triplicate fest was that it’s too bad the air travel ground stop didn’t last another week. Trump’s international trips are like an endless Matryoshka doll, with each subsequent international humiliation being worse than the last. And this one was that, times three. The axis of evil has been replaced by the dictatorial triple threat, and the American president is an enthusiastic member of the troika. The whole style over substance affair could, I suppose, be viewed as a win, win, win. Xi got to look like the host with the most leader of the world. Putin, a murderous mafia boss of a semi-failed state, got images that make him look like he’s on equal footing with the world’s superpowers. And Trump got to fawn over his frenemies, in addition to bringing his traveling one-man slumber party to an international audience. I don’t blame him for being tired. Betrayal is more exhausting than it looks. Never judge a man until you’ve walked a mile on his bone spurs. Sadly, with all that winning, no one was at the summit to represent American interests. The land of the free was replaced by the land of the three. Oh well, you win some you threesome. I’d like to be more positive, but you can’t polish a third.

+ Here’s the excellent Anne Applebaum with a look at some of the trilateral collateral. “Its true purpose was not to end any wars—and certainly not to end Russia’s bloody invasion of Ukraine—but to produce propaganda photographs and video clips that each of the three leaders will now use to mask their political failures. Certainly this was President Trump’s main goal. Before the three leaders met, he actually told Fox News that the most significant moment was already over: ‘the greeting yesterday, which in the history of China has never happened.’ Xi Jinping, aware of how easy it is to manipulate the American president, had met Trump at his airplane, on the tarmac … For Vladimir Putin, the meeting also created useful propaganda. Now almost five years into a war he believed he would win in three days, he is coping with 1.5 million war casualties; the loss, as of this week, of half of his country’s oil-refining capacity; and even, in the past few days, the destruction of the Kerch Strait Bridge, which links Russia to Crimea … Nevertheless, Putin will use the Shenzhen meeting to tell Russians that their country is still a superpower, still allowed to sit in the same room as the Americans and the Chinese … For Xi, the meeting was useful because he was the host, he set up the photographs, and his propaganda was broadcast around the world. With Trump’s cooperation, he telegraphed American decline, Chinese power, and Russian subservience.” Trump’s Embarrassing, Inconsequential Summit.

+ “Mr. Trump, who has spoken for years with admiration about both autocrats, gushed about being welcomed by the two men. ‘We are really making history,’ he said at their meeting.” (Nothing has gone down in history quite as fast as America’s international leadership role under Trump.) (Gift Article): Behind Trump Meeting, Xi and Putin Share a Vision of Usurping U.S. Power.

+ It really was all worse than I’m making it sound. Especially the sick love Trump showed for Putin, his “friend” with whom he has a “great relationship.” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk responded with this: “God, protect us from such friends.”

One of the more anticipated IPOs in years has finally taken place as Anthropic hit the public markets. The stock initially soared well above its offering price, but then Claude thawed, and it has since settled into more traditional, solid first-day performance. The rest of the market suffered another rough day. Here’s the latest: Anthropic Shares Climb After Multibillion-Dollar I.P.O. “Anthropic has become by far the most valuable company on the stock market with the legal designation of a public benefit corporation, or P.B.C. That status requires Anthropic to prioritize its corporate mission — to develop safe artificial intelligence systems ‘for the long-term benefit of humanity.'” (If, you know, humanity survives the long term.)

At the risk of bringing back memories of the great toilet paper rush of 2020, I should let you know that the tech outages of the past week have driven some panic buying at Costco and Walmart. Generators are a big hit, as is general pantry loading. (But if the internet goes down, is there still a point in living?) The prepper crowd is way ahead of the rest of us. But the rest of us are starting to join the prepper crowd. “Once written off as paranoid fantasy, and largely the domain of those with conservative and libertarian views, prepping itself has rapidly joined the mainstream and, in some quarters, has taken on a liberal bent: Rather than hiding away alone, armed to the teeth, there is an emphasis on building resilience and connections among people.” (Gift Article): They’re Prepping for a Broken Digital World. “DoorDash is not an emergency plan.” (Of course not. You need to back it up with UberEats and GrubHub.)

+ “We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments. The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyberattacks. Bad actors are using open-weight models and new agentic frameworks to find and exploit vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale.” Palo Alto Networks CEO just dropped a truth bomb on the network outages.

+ As I explained yesterday, while it looks like our computers weren’t hacked, the events of the last week made it plainly clear that have been.

While some of us are stocking up on toilet paper, others still don’t have access to toilets. And it just happens to be World Toilet Day, a funny idea with a serious goal. “The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.” And from Chris Mims in the (Gift Article): I Tried New York City’s New High-Tech Public Bathrooms—and Saw the Future. “On a day-long tour of New York City’s new, high-tech public bathrooms this week, I found them remarkably tidy—as did the many New Yorkers whom I cornered both before and after they used them.” (Being immediately confronted by a reporter after using a public restroom sounds like something out of an IBS nightmare.)

Iowa Chu Talking About, Willis? “The U.S. Army’s plan to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unstable and might explode if moved has some Iowa residents worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems. The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is set for Friday, and officials recommend that some residents in nearby Middletown vacate the area. If they can’t leave their homes, they should stay inside and keep windows and doors closed.” (Even though they also warn that the blast could break some windows.) Iowans brace for a lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals.

+ Turn Your Head and Witkoff: “SEC filings reveal that the president’s son-in-law is negotiating for peace while profiting from war.” Jared Kushner’s Undisclosed Investment. (In fairness, I don’t think Jared has an official government role.)

+ What the Heil is He Talking About? (Robot voice) Attention plebeians and other human life forms, I am not MAGA and was never really MAGA. Please save this data to your hard drive. Elon Musk claims ‘I’m not MAGA‘ and says he regrets vast sums to back Republicans. (Well, I believe the second part…)

+ After a year during which her megahit Choosin’ Texas dominated the charts, “Ella Langley set a new, all-time record for the most CMA Awards wins in one night on Wednesday.” But my favorite milestone of the night was achieved by NextDraft-approved artist Stephen Wilson Jr, who won best new artist at the age of 47. Here’s his CMA performance with Chris Stapleton. A decade ago, he was a scientist shepherding the creation of a digestible dental-cleaning chew for dogs. Years after leaving that gig for a full-time music career, he burst onto the scene in 2024 with this viral cover of Stand by Me.

items.title: Trust Fall is in the Error
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
We’ve been hacked. I’m not talking about the Microsoft downtime, the air travel grounding, the bank inaccessibility, the Apple outage, or the fact that, for about 45 minutes this morning, my NextDraft pun generator wasn’t working. The more we learn, the more it looks like those software snafus were likely due to attempted upgrades, ill-advised patches, and endeavors aimed at AI-enabling communication systems that were originally built with two cans and a long string. But while it looks like our computers weren’t hacked, the last week made it plainly clear that have been. We didn’t know what was going on during these tech failures, and when we were given a series of explanations by the hack jobs in the administration, we didn’t believe them. And why would we? They lie as a matter of policy. They lie every time they speak. The truth has systematically been twisted into a pile of misinformation more tangled than the box of old plugs, cables, and cords you never got around to throwing out. As George W Bush famously explained: “Fool me once, shame on — shame on you. Fool me — you can’t get fooled again.” In an age defined by isolation and loneliness, Billy Joel may have prophesied the loneliest thing of all when he sang: Honesty is such a lonely word. So, when you hear the administration-offered statements like Marco Rubio’s proclamation that “there’s ‘zero’ information that U.S. outages are caused by a malign actor,” you’re right to have zero certainty they’re telling the truth. You’re getting that explanation a malign actor. You don’t trust them because they’ve spent years intentionally hacking your trust to smithereens. We have been trust-falled into the deepest bowels of hell. At this point, even Charlie Brown wouldn’t try to kick a football held by anyone in this administration. And that’s why I’m trying to explain that the biggest hack of this era is that we’re all worried our government is lying to us about the causes of the outages. Trust is glitching. Trust has been hijacked. Our democracy’s terms of service have been rewritten, and our citizenry is no longer willing to blindly click to agree. I’d suggest that when it comes to matters of IT, you’d be better off getting explanations from tech companies than from the administration, but we don’t trust tech companies either.

+ Nicole Perlroth wrote the book on cybersecurity (So, yes, you can trust her), and she shared some thoughts on X: “We were told to ‘move fast and break things.’ VCs told us to celebrate the idea that ‘software would eat the world.’ Now we’re telling ourselves we can simply ‘roll out AI’ across everything, as though nothing underneath will buckle. We never stopped to ask: SHOULD WE? … Nobody ever asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?”

+ With enough work and time and the right leaders, there may still be time to rebuild the trust upon which democracy depends. But that could change if Grand Theft Auto VI goes down, too.

“Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name and completing a political comeback in a state President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins.” Democrat Mary Peltola wins US Senate race in Alaska. (Maybe Trump did make one true statement. I’m almost getting tired of all the winning.)

+ The Second Dan Sullivan Made No Impact on Alaska Senate Race. (Let that be a lesson to all future campaign strategists. If you want a real impact, you’re gonna need at least three Dan Sullivans.)

“‘Down with the ,’ people shouted, referring to the entrenched patronage networks that reward party loyalty over merit in nearly every sphere of life. When another group chanted a World War II slogan—’Albania for the Albanians, death to the traitors’—my fixer said, ‘This one is for you.’ He meant Americans. What had first sparked the protests, in May, were plans by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of the American president, to build an ultra-luxury resort in a fragile nature preserve in the country’s south, where flamingos gather.” Ariel Sabar in (Gift Article): How Jared Kushner Sparked a Revolution in the Balkans. (The midterms may be the first step toward America forgiving itself for Trumpism. It’s gonna take the rest of the world a lot longer.)

That which doesn’t kill the regime makes it stronger? … “The mood was something I’d never encountered here before. Not shock and awe, but shock and dread. The dread comes from the dawning awareness that this latest war with Iran, started by America and Israel, is going to end with Iran more dominant than ever over its neighbors. The Gulf Arabs never urged the United States to start this war, but once it did, they assumed it had a plan to finish it.” Thomas Friedman in the (Gift Article): Shock and Dread in the Gulf. “The prevailing sentiment was most pointedly conveyed to me by an Eastern European diplomat at the conference, citing an aphorism from Cold War days: ‘The trouble with being an ally of the United States is that you never know when it will turn around and stab itself in the back.'”

“In a 7-mile-wide city of barely 800,000 people, the AI boom has minted thousands of fortunes worth $10 million or more, many of them at the two biggest companies. At the midpoint of Anthropic’s IPO price range, its average employee would each own shares worth $72 million, according to a (Gift Article) analysis of PitchBook data. The average OpenAI insider’s stake is worth almost $126 million, based on the firm’s most recent valuation.” Anthropic’s IPO Is Igniting a Massive AI Wealth Boom in San Francisco. (This gold rush is so massive, we may have to change the name of our football team to the San Francisco 26ers.)

+ Meet and Greet (and Beat): “In a rare and surprising move, Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of historic three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin. It is believed to be the first time that Xi, in power for more than a decade, has been on hand to greet any foreign leader arriving in China.” (Oh, man, he’s really gonna try to get one over on Trump this time…)

+ “I learned that I’m overly credulous when it comes to men’s stated intentions (‘You can recognize that a man is unavailable, evasive, selfish, or inconsistent,’ the bot said, ‘and nevertheless continue to treat his expressions of desire as evidence that something more meaningful might develop’) and that I’m looking for love in all the wrong places (‘You sometimes recognize a man’s limitations but behave as though they are negotiable’). Anna Holmes in (Gift Article): ChatGPT Analyzed 32,245 of My Text Messages.

+ Sean Duffy Stars in The Real World: “I have a great idea. Let’s take that money in $100 bills and have a national weenie roast instead. It will be a lot more fun and about as effective in fixing the existing air traffic control system … Like upgrading a Model T for a highway, overhauling the air traffic control system architecture will never be able to achieve sufficient airspeed.” $50 Billion Won’t Fix Air Traffic Control. It Needs to Be Scrapped. (Can we maybe scrap it at a moment when I’m not on a flight?) Speaking of Model Ts and highways, California has banned Waymo self-driving cars from freeways.

+ Caviar Wishes and Abstain Dreams: Almost nobody’s vying for an invite to Trump’s second meme coin dinner. “In the run-up to the first gala, in May 2025, Trump’s coin was riding high. Some bought millions of dollars worth of coins to attend, and it took at least $55,000 worth of coin holdings to score an invite. This time, however, one prescient buyer earned an invite for just $518.” (He’s still overpaying.)

AI is cool and all, but is an invention: “The novelty streetwear garment was designed to keep burritos both warm and concealed while sneaking them into the cinema for illicit mid-movie snacking.” (Forget the cinema. I’m getting one of these to sneak a second burrito into my man cave.)

items.title: None of This Computes
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
The new meaning of Singularity is when only one of your tech services is still working. It’s been a rough week in tech, and I’m not talking about Jensen Huang’s seven-year itch glitch. For a warm-up, Microsoft had a massive outage that made email inaccessible for millions. Then there was that little router upgrade in Arkansas that grounded planes across the country. People were finally able to fly home, only to realize that they were temporarily unable to access their bank accounts. Today, Apple has confirmed an iCloud outage, affecting Apple Pay and other services. All of these issues, we’ve been told, have been due to unrelated software bugs or bad updates. But we’re all so dependent on technology, it’s hard not to worry that something more nefarious is afoot. Even harder when the week of crazy tech headlines has led to this one from CNN: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down, sources say. I’m hoping the timing of all these snafus is just a weird coincidence. But I’m still considering this to be a tech apocalypse level Defcon 3. (Defcon 1 is when Netflix stops streaming.)

+ Luckily, we have just the leadership in place to manage these issues and give us assurances we can trust. “President Donald Trump brushed off recent mass outages that wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails … ‘It’s life, it’s life … ‘When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.'” OK, now may be a good time to back up your data … and your democracy. (I wonder if the nation’s technology stack can be rebooted by someone with bone spurs in his foot?)

My son was born around the time the first iPhone was released, so he’s really never had my full attention. Of course, he’s also never had full attention. I doubt he, or anyone else, will be surprised that the latest data indicates the school phone bans around the country are gradually leading to improved test scores. “Schools with strict bans — requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found.” I’m not sure that positioning these results as being the equivalent of more school is the best way to get buy-in from young people, but we all know that it’s better to put your phone in a locker than to check your brain at the door. But what if turning off technology required doing the latter? The interface between the brain and computing is the next frontier, and like many new technologies, the possibilities are both breathtakingly awesome and incredibly disturbing. J. Galen Buckwalter has already had experiences across the spectrum. He regularly allows “a researcher to attach wires to three metal knobs screwed into his skull like a cyberpunk mohawk. The wires connect to six chips that were implanted in his brain during a seven-hour craniotomy. They record his neural signals — the firing of his brain when he thinks, speaks or moves — and transmit them to a computer to be analyzed.” He’s hoping the technology can be of assistance to him (he’s almost totally paralyzed) and others: “Brain-computer interfaces have enabled people with paralysis to fly drones and helped people who have lost the ability to speak to communicate — using just their thoughts. Eventually, researchers say, they could allow the regulation of emotions such as pain or fear; the instant transfer of knowledge, such as a new language; or the merging of human consciousness with artificial intelligence.” (That escalated quickly.) Buckwalter has also learned that some of the same data handling issues that have come up on the internet are now coming up in his brain, as data ownership of your gray matter is a particularly gray area. (Gift Article): Does This Man Have a Right to the Data From His Own Brain? What do you think about all this? Actually, don’t tell me. We’ll find out soon enough.

“China is the principal backer of Russia’s war against Ukraine, providing essential supplies that keep Moscow’s missiles and drones flying. Russia is giving Iran satellite imaging and overhead targeting data even as Iran strikes U.S. military assets in the Gulf region. Chinese companies have provided Iran with crucial missile components. Joint Chinese and Russian military exercises in the western Pacific are increasingly active around Japan and near contested island territories. Beneath the appearance of accord at the trilateral summit, Mr. Trump will be making nice with opponents who have daggers drawn against our allies and partners in three of the world’s most dangerous spots.” So you get it, right? These are not our allies. But not everyone gets it. (Gift Article): Trump’s Ego Trip With Xi and Putin Will End Badly. (On the plus side, Trump’s Asia trip got off to a spirited start in Manila, where he was greeted with a rousing rendition of YMCA. We’ve never been so respected!)

+ To the extent there are any serious negotiations at this summit, they might be between factions inside the Trump administration. (Gift Article): Trump Administration Divide on China Policy Breaks Into Public View. (It can be broken down as a battle between those who want to partially sell out American interests for personal gain and to appease the president, and those who want to fully sell out American interests for the same reasons.) “Amid the fallout, Mr. Trump has appeared more concerned in public about offending Mr. Xi than about the risks to national security.”

Jensen Huang has agreed to talk with House lawmakers trying to get to the bottom of exactly how much Nvidia shared with, and sold to, China. He’s also agreed to come back as CEO if you really, really want him to. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” (It’s this kind of smooth, sweet-talking that got him into this mess in the first place.)

+ “The records illustrate that the couple operated on both sides of the U.S.-China technology divide: Chinese state money was invested in Kang’s domestic ventures as his wife’s overseas company gained access to the chips Washington was trying to keep out of China. Kang connected those worlds, having known Jensen Huang from both men’s days in the videogame industry. Kang told people who know the couple that he had introduced his wife to Jensen and that he appeared to accept their romantic relationship.” (Gift Article): Alice Huang’s Husband Built a Data-Center Empire Backed by the Chinese State.

“New US intelligence indicates that Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC, even as officials continue to debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute such a plot.” (Is the leak of this information more reality, politics, or strategy? All answers are worrisome, some more than others.)

+ Troubled Bridge Over Water: “Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an ‘unprecedented’ military operation.”

+ “I found no hidden explanation for what had happened to him. As best as I could establish, Sanchez is set to spend the next 30 years in prison simply for moving a box of radical zines.” (Gift Article): 30 Years for Moving a Box.

+ “To commemorate The New York Times’s 175th anniversary, The New York Times Magazine set for itself an impossible project: to select the 10 most consequential days since the paper began publishing.” Ten Days That Changed the World. (About 15 years ago, five or so folks from the NYT came to my office in SF to get my advice about their newsletter strategy. Not sure how that meeting didn’t make this list…)

+ “Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off … She didn’t have to worry: Her boss admitted that he was taking time off for the same reason. ‘I don’t think the company’s even going to be up and running for probably two or three days,’ Rogers told me. If you’ve got a metal roof that needs replacing in south-central Texas, it just might have to wait.” The release of the new Grand Theft Auto game could result in The Least Productive Day of the Year.

items.title: The Bile High Club
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
Imagine being stuck on a grounded plane and suddenly remembering that the person in charge of Homeland Security is a guy named Markwayne. That was the experience for millions of travelers who faced a grounding of flights across America on Friday. And all those routes may have been brought down by a single router in Arkansas. (Gift Article): How Could a Router Lead to a Nationwide Ground Stop? “Aviation experts said it was likely that when the new router came online in Arkansas, the device began to send so much information that it overwhelmed the older equipment, which could not respond fast enough. That led to a cascade of issues.” The cascade of issues was followed by a cascade of blame deflection as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy went on just about every Sunday morning talk show to refuse to apologize for the sky-emptying error, while Trump (surprise, surprise) blamed Biden. (By the time this is over, Trump and Duffy will be blaming the Wright Brothers.) At one point, Markwayne Mullin explained, “They were putting (in) new equipment and new technology. It was overwhelming the older system.” (That’s sort of how democracy felt after our entire leadership was replaced by characters from the movie, .) And when they say older technology, they’re not kidding. Here’s a headline from ten days ago: FAA to finally ditch floppy disks in what it calls ‘historic’ tech upgrade. How old is this tech? When pilots start up a 747, the system says, “You’ve got mail!” On some level, we have no idea whether this nightmare was caused by an Arkansas router, new technology overwhelming older technology, floppy disks flipping out, or something more nefarious, because the people providing us with the updates lie every time they speak. It’s enough to make you want to cancel your flights and just drive to your destination. Unfortunately, gas is too expensive for that.

“Lemmy and Iggy, two carrion crows, are no strangers to a psychology lab. As study participants, they have helped scientists prove that birds can use tools to forage, learn numbers and count objects, and provided other insights into the ways birds think. Now, they’ve also revealed that birds can make staggeringly quick decisions, besting their human and nonhuman primate counterparts with ease.” (Gift Article): ‘Birdbrain’ Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can. (And they don’t fall from the sky during software updates.)

“A group of senior American officers, worried about exactly the type of attack that killed those six soldiers in Kuwait, told me they repeatedly urged commanders in the Middle East to deploy the new Ukrainian technology. The Pentagon ignored their warnings, which included detailed reports sent up the chain of command. Several of the officers who tried to raise the alarm about Iranian Shaheds have since been fired or forced into early retirement.” Simon Shuster in (Gift Article): The Pentagon Ignored a Warning About the Danger of Iran’s Drones.

+ “Confirming a new GAO director as the GOP’s majority wanes would be a tremendous gift to President Donald Trump. Fights over federal spending will surely dominate the next two years and rushing through a pliant watchdog willing to turn a blind eye to Trump’s blatant seizure of funds would only further enable his illegality.” Trump getting his handpicked Government Accountability Office director confirmed would ensure that every spending bill Democrats pass is treated as a suggestion.

+ Chopsticking the Landing: “Yesterday, for the first time ever, engineers successfully pulled off a —using the company’s Mechazilla tower’s ‘chopstick’ arms to snatch a starship the size of a skyscraper out of the sky after it had spent the past 22 hours in Earth’s orbit.” Not all air travel tech is outdated. (Gift Article): Awesome. (Some great video.)

+ Carbon Emissions of Biggest U.S. Data Centers Already Rival Entire Countries. “The largest data centers in the United States are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually — almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark.” (Well, then, it’s pretty simple. We’re gonna have to get rid of Bolivia and Denmark.)

+ His name is Pattinson. Robert Pattinson. And he’s the next James Bond. (I say no. My wife says yes. So it’s probably a good choice.)

+ “Raye leads all nominees with a startling 11 nods, followed by Rosalía with nine. Tied for seven nominations each are Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers.” Grammy Nominations 2027.

+ “One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick’s Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.” (Oh, Florida, you should have gone blue.)

+ Joe Rogan says Trump ‘lost most of the country‘ after the midterms. (Man who guided citizens over cliff now reports that the ground below is hard.)

items.title: The Pay Dirt
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
You can pay me now or you can pay me later. You can pay layaway, you can pay on credit, you can pay out of pocket, you can pay through the nose, you can pay an arm and a leg, you can pay dues, respects, dearly, heed, homage, lip service, compliments, cash on the barrelhead, the piper, peanuts, under the table, over the table, the ultimate price, or you can gladly pay me Tuesday. In the shadow of an election that was all about affordability, it seems like the last thing you need is a new way to pay. But agentic AI is here, and one of its supposedly excellent features is that it creates a new way to separate you from your money, and you don’t even have to be part of the process. You give the agent your credit card or banking info, and it will go out and manage transactions for you. That might sound like a big leap for consumers, but it’s a bigger leap for those on the receiving end of those payments (United Airlines is the latest company to ban AI agents), and an even bigger leap (and concern) for the industry that has been built over decades to manage those transactions. “Meta’s Muse, Instinct and other personal AI assistants have been empowered in recent weeks to make purchases on behalf of cardholders, marking new steps toward a potential future where consumers no longer need to initiate a purchase or press ‘buy’ at checkout. That is generating buzz and excitement about AI bots’ ability to create a new world order in payments. But inside banks and other payments companies and merchants, worries abound about the implications and whether bots will lead to elevated cases of fraud and returns, and open new legal risks. Early camps are already being formed.” (Gift Article): AI bots are using credit cards. Banks are racing to keep up. (alt link). “The systems that power payments today are built on byzantine rules, fraud protections, federal laws and network and bank fees that aren’t intended for robots. This ecosystem has long been in a state of constant tension between merchants, networks that set fees and rules, and card issuers that extend credit to consumers. Move one piece or change one fee even by a cent and the impact can quickly ripple into billions of dollars won and lost.” (I’d hold off on sharing your financial information with agents until things shake out and we know the systems are safe. There’s no need to turn your piggy bank into a guinea pig. You can pay me no mind, but excellent advice like this is why they pay me the big bucks.)

The fallout from the Nvidia story continues to take a toll on our psyches (and our portfolios). From (Gift Article): ‘I’m a Piece of Sh-t’: Jensen Huang’s Last Hours as Nvidia CEO. (With that kind of self-contempt, he should really consider writing a daily newsletter). From Stephen Witt in the (Gift Article): I Wrote Jensen Huang’s Biography. Here’s What Led to His Downfall. “When I wrote my biography of Mr. Huang, I titled it ‘The Thinking Machine.’ The name referred to the microchips that powered A.I., but also to Mr. Huang’s marauding, relentless intellect, which never slowed down or turned off. In the wake of his stunning departure, spurred by revelations that he carried on at least two affairs, one with a woman whom U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, and another with one of his direct reports, I should write a sequel: ‘The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine.'”

+ As much as this is a business story and a corporate leadership lesson, the more we learn, the more we’ll realize that this is first and foremost a political scandal of Trumpian proportions. It goes right to the top, so someone on the way up has gotta take the fall. And anyone following the leaks can see the knives are out for the commerce secretary. Howard Lutnick under pressure over alleged lack of action. (The one good thing about this administration is that no matter who gets punished for something, they deserve it.)

+ “In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China.” But not until Trump loaded up on Nvidia stock. (You just grab them by the portfolio. When you’re president, they just let you do it.)

+ “One lesson of the Jensen Huang scandal is that policy makers gave extraordinary influence to technology executives whose commercial interests did not always align with American interests. His departure offers a rare opportunity to rethink the assumptions that have underpinned AI strategy for the past two years, address mounting concerns about the technology, and establish a new approach that protects both American AI leadership and public safety.” Thomas Wright in (Gift Article): The Jensen Huang Scandal Should Change Everything. Don’t get your hopes up. is doing a lot of work in that headline.

+ And if you missed it yesterday, I covered everything from the data center-sized portfolio losses, to the megawatt-powered affairs, to the unfair hit to the leather-wearing community: The Honey Trapdoor.

“Fox News’ fixation on the league dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t consume Fox News myself. The first clue came at a family gathering. A conservative relative started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark while parroting right-wing conspiracy theories about Black players. This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.” A very interesting analysis about how the pathetic jerks at Fox News can spoil anything, even something as awesome and uplifting as the WNBA. Melanie Walsh with Jan Diehm in : Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA? This is about one sport, but it’s really about the way Fox News covers everything, and it will help explain where your crazy uncle got the ideas he’ll be sharing over Thanksgiving dinner.

Black Doves on Netflix, starring Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw, is like The Diplomat, meets Slow Horses, meets John Wick. It’s fun and fast-paced, and season two is better than season one (especially the addition of Ambika Mod).

+ In a follow-up to his excellent novel , Chad Harbach returns to the fictional campus of Westish College in his new and excellent novel, The Brightness. As Tom Perrotta says, “The Brightness is a monumental campus novel, full of smart and mercurial characters who feel as real as your own roommates.” (I swear, my freshman year college roommate was the president of the Berkeley Young Republicans. I once accidentally walked in on him and his girlfriend having sex. And I’ve been a Democrat ever since…)

“A river boat with over 100 passengers was struck on Friday by a much larger tanker ship, capsizing the cruise vessel and prompting a major rescue effort in the Mississippi River near the French Quarter.” The video and images from the scene are crazy. Rescue operations are underway. Here’s the latest.

+ A One Point Five Alarm Fire: “Scientists for years have warned that allowing global average temperatures to rise 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above preindustrial levels would result in a profoundly more dangerous world. Extreme heat will become more common and more intense. Storms will become more powerful and destructive. Sea levels will rise. And poor countries will bear the brunt of the damage.” At this point, 1.5 is a pipe dream (and the temperature inside that pipe just set a record). A Key Paris Agreement Goal Is Dead. What Now?

+ After the warnings about AI destroying humanity, it was good old email that overpowered the system. A negative Outlook: Microsoft scrambles to fix email outage. “Very little is known so far about what is behind the outage, but Microsoft has attributed it to an ‘elevated load,’ or servers becoming overstretched. The tech giant assured users it was doing everything it could to fix the problem.” (I’d write an inappropriate pun about elevated loads, but I’m spent after a week of Nvidia jokes.)

+ “Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced on Thursday that he would challenge Senator Chuck Schumer of New York for majority leader, setting up a clash among Democrats just as they were celebrating their new majority.” (Infighting is Dems celebrate!)

+ Muting the Executioner’s Song: The excellent Bryan Stevenson in the (Gift Article): “The death penalty in America is not about whether people deserve to die for the crimes they commit; it is about whether our imperfect governments deserve to kill. Gov. Gavin Newsom’s commutation last week of all of California’s 548 death sentences to life imprisonment without parole is a remarkable act of moral leadership.”

+ “Matt Lambert, a former emergency room physician and health care technology executive, shot five people and then himself on Thursday in D.C., apparently motivated by a bitter, ongoing and all-consuming legal dispute with the Metropole Condominium Association and the building’s property manager.” Michael Brice-Saddler in : What the Logan Circle Shooter Told Me.

items.title: The Honey Trapdoor
items.author: Dave Pell
items.content:
Jensen Huang had sex with multiple partners, but somehow my portfolio got screwed. When it comes to Nvidia, I got in early. And I stayed in. I’m not a promiscuous trader who goes in and out, in and out. And until this week, that loyalty had paid off. Like millions of stock owners, I wish I had pulled out earlier. In fairness, nobody thought the AI’s most engorged bubble would ultimately be popped like a cheap condom by the most human of desires. I still have no idea how a guy at the center of the company at the center of the industry at the center of the global economy had the vigor and spare time to juggle numerous affairs (not to mention Donald Trump’s ego). This guy was managing the most important company in the world while managing multiple romantic partners. I’ve seen 100 megawatt data centers that burn less energy. What was he trying to do, run for president? Seriously, if Huang had any more sex out of wedlock, he’d have to rename his company X. Everyone knows the number one rule in business is that you don’t have more partners than your company. I know this seems like a lot of cheap jokes, but after this week’s hit to my portfolio, I can no longer afford the expensive ones. And I’m not the only one. Everyone had Nvidia in their portfolios. And now the thrill is gone. And so is the trill (several of them, actually). I can’t remember if it was Warren Buffett, Milton Friedman, or John Maynard Keynes who said, “Don’t tap that if it will tap the market cap.” Now, Nvidia board members are left to Purell themselves as they feverishly search for a new leader to replace their supposedly irreplaceable old one, who just issued his resignation (although, I’m guessing the board pressed Ctrl-Shift-Esc before Huang pressed Command-Q).

+ Until today, the government was telling us that we can’t drive a Polestar or buy a DJI drone, but it’s fine if Nvidia sells chips to China. And the tech industry that has been telling us that we need to risk our very existence to stay ahead of the Chinese in the AI race initially tried to brush off Huang sharing secrets with a spy as no big deal. Up is down and wrong is right in the age of corruption. Jensen Huang’s resignation means the full story is probably a lot worse than what we already know. It also suggests that there are still lines that can’t be crossed (except when it comes to the administration, whose involvement in this is likely a bigger scandal than the scandal). Now comes the hardest part. Finding a new AI CEO whom people trust when AI CEOs have spent so much time convincing us they’re not to be trusted. Whoever gets the gig is going to have some big shoes — and a lot of little leather jackets — to fill. Trump says that Tim Apple should become Timvidia. But Trump himself is heavily implicated in this disaster. I’d rather see Tim Cook replace him. (If Cook says no to Nvidia, maybe Trump will suggest Dana White for the job.)

+ Meanwhile, the Justice Department has launched several investigations into purported honey-trapping spy Alice Huang. But the people at the very top of the administration were warned about her a long time ago.

+ “It has been a hard week, even for the thick-skinned. The news that Jensen Huang, a co-founder of Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence regards as a Chinese spy, has shaken not only Silicon Valley and geopolitics. It also has been an earthquake for the leather-jacket-wearing community.” Jensen Huang Betrayed the Leather Jacket Community. You can run, but you can’t rawhide.

There was a joke going around the internet that the reason it was taking so long to get the final election numbers from Mississippi is because they have to count, One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, Three Mississippi. Whatever took so long, it was worth the wait. Scott Colom’s “shocking upset victory in a state where Donald Trump won by 23 points in 2024 is even more remarkable considering Mississippi’s history. This was the state where Jim Crow was the most violent and repressive. It was where Emmett Till was lynched, Evers was assassinated, and the young civil rights workers James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan. There were 581 documented lynchings during the Jim Crow era, more than any other state.” Mississippi Elects Its First Black Senator Since Reconstruction. “Before the passage of the Voting Rights Act, only 6.7 percent of eligible Black voters were registered to vote in Mississippi. Now, more than 60 years later, it was Black voters who turned out in record numbers to rewrite the history books, motivated in part by a new struggle to protect voting rights.”

+ “It was Mr. Hudson’s father who was initially cast in the campaign ad mocking a suggestion from Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, that Mississippi residents pick another type of protein to avoid rising beef prices. When the elder Mr. Hudson balked at a script that would require him to utter profanity on camera, his son volunteered.” The Man at the Center of Scott Colom’s Protein Ad. (And shee-it, that ad helped change history.)

“These settlement numbers, reported for the first time, provide a rare glimpse into what the companies are willing to pay to avoid high-profile trials with teen users — and the looming financial risk such cases present. Roughly 9,800 personal injury cases are pending in state and federal court against Meta, Google’s YouTube, Snap Inc. and TikTok Inc.” (Gift Article): The Confidential Payments Meta and TikTok Made to Addicted Teens. “Seven confidential deals with young plaintiffs ranged from $2 million to $2.5 million. And the remaining personal injury lawsuits could expose the companies to billions of dollars in liability.”

“Air travel has become so safe in large part because of a profound commitment from the people in charge to learn from tragedies — what aviation experts call ‘lessons written in blood’ … But the Trump administration has displayed an extraordinary unwillingness to learn new lessons, and in some cases it seems to be unlearning the old ones.” James Fallows in the (Gift Article): Is Air Travel Getting Less Safe?

+ Nothing to Write Home About: “The last time sales were this low was August 2010 when the economy was still reeling from the housing bust and the recession that followed.” (Gift Article): Home Sales in October Plummet to 16-Year Low.

+ “Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth awarded the soldier who reprimanded him and members of his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier a Joint Service Commendation Medal on Thursday.” (He must have been embarrassed to award someone he’d ordinarily fire.) After hearing voices and laughter, Specialist Iglesias of The Old Guard yelled, “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”

“​In its glory days, the S.S. United States was fast, luxurious and all but indestructible. As the ocean liner’s designer, William Francis Gibbs, liked to ​say, ‘You can’t set her on fire, you can’t sink her, and you can’t catch her.’ And he was right, up to a point. On Wednesday one of the greatest ships to sail the seas made its final journey, 180 feet down to the bottom of the ocean.​” The S.S. United States, a Historic Supership, Sinks to the Ocean Floor. But the metaphor doesn’t stop there. It was sunk in the Gulf of Mexico…
